excerpt: One-half, 0.5 and 50% are the same number wearing three different outfits. Here is how I teach Grade 6 students to switch between fractions, decimals and percents without freezing — plus a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write ½ on the board, then 0.5, then 50%, and ask a Grade 6 class if they are the same. You will get a split vote every time. That hesitation is the whole reason fractions decimals and percents grade 6 work matters: these three forms are just different costumes for one number, and a student who can swap between them at will has cracked a skill that runs straight through Class 7 ratios, Class 8 discounts and every competitive exam after. This is not the Fractions chapter or the Percentage chapter on its own — it is the bridge between them.

There are exactly six conversions to learn, because three forms pair up in six directions. Most students only ever get taught three or four and then guess the rest. Below I walk through all six, the way I teach them to a mixed-ability class in a Tier-2 school, with the one shortcut per direction that actually sticks.

The six conversions, one at a time

Fraction to decimal

Divide the top by the bottom. That is the entire rule. For ¾, work out 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. The catch students trip on: they divide 4 by 3 out of habit because 4 is bigger. Say it out loud — ‘numerator divided by denominator’ — until it becomes automatic.

Decimal to fraction

Read the place value, then simplify. 0.6 is ‘six tenths’ = 6/10 = 3/5. 0.25 is ‘twenty-five hundredths’ = 25/100 = ¼. The number of decimal places tells you how many zeros go under the line: one place means tenths, two means hundredths.

Decimal to percent

Multiply by 100, or just slide the decimal point two places right. 0.375 becomes 37.5%. This is the easiest of the six and I teach it first for a quick early win.

Percent to decimal

Divide by 100, or slide the point two places left. 8% becomes 0.08. Watch the single-digit percents — students write 0.8 for 8% far too often. A percent under 10 must have a zero after the point.

Fraction to percent

Two routes. Either turn the fraction into a decimal first and then shift the point (¾ → 0.75 → 75%), or multiply the fraction by 100 directly. For ⅖, that is 2/5 × 100 = 40%. I prefer the decimal route because it reuses a skill they already have.

Percent to fraction

Put the percent over 100, then simplify. 60% = 60/100 = 3/5. 12.5% = 12.5/100 — clear the decimal by writing 125/1000 = ⅛. That last one always earns a gasp.

Comparing and ordering mixed forms

Here is where marks are won and lost. A question hands you ⅗, 0.55 and 58% and asks you to put them in order. The mistake is trying to compare them as they are. The fix is a rule I drill hard:

  • Pick one common form — decimals are usually easiest.
  • Convert every number to that form: ⅗ = 0.6, 0.55 stays, 58% = 0.58.
  • Now compare like with like: 0.55 < 0.58 < 0.6.
  • Translate the order back to the original forms: 0.55, 58%, ⅗.

Decimals win as the common form because they line up on a place-value chart and the comparison becomes visual. Percents are the second-best choice. Comparing raw fractions with different denominators is the slowest route — avoid it unless the denominators are already the same.

A counter-intuitive tip

Bigger-looking is not bigger. Students assume 0.9 is smaller than 0.85 because 85 feels like more than 9. Pad the shorter decimal with a zero — 0.90 versus 0.85 — and the truth is obvious. This one habit prevents a huge share of ordering errors.

A realistic practice routine

Ten focused minutes a day beats a two-hour cram. Monday and Tuesday on the six conversions in isolation, Wednesday on the memory table, Thursday on ordering mixed sets, and the weekend on a mixed worksheet where the student has to decide which conversion each question needs. That deciding step — not the arithmetic — is what the exam actually tests. One honest caveat: do not push speed before accuracy. A student who converts 12.5% to ⅛ slowly but correctly is in far better shape than one who guesses fast.

faq.q: What are the six conversions a Grade 6 student must know?
faq.a: Fraction to decimal, decimal to fraction, decimal to percent, percent to decimal, fraction to percent and percent to fraction. Learning all six — not just three or four — is what lets a student handle any mixed-form question.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to compare fractions, decimals and percents?
faq.a: Convert everything to decimals first, because decimals line up on place value and are quick to compare. Pad shorter decimals with a zero so 0.9 reads as 0.90 — that stops the classic error of thinking 0.85 is bigger than 0.9.

faq.q: How do I turn a fraction into a percent?
faq.a: Either convert the fraction to a decimal and slide the point two places right (¾ → 0.75 → 75%), or multiply the fraction by 100 directly. Both give the same answer — use whichever feels faster to you.

faq.q: Which common values should my child memorise?
faq.a: The high-frequency ones: ½ = 0.5 = 50%, ¼ = 0.25 = 25%, ¾ = 0.75 = 75%, ⅕ = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5% and 1/3 ≈ 0.333 = 33.3%. Memorising these speeds up mixed-form questions noticeably.
